name: Zomato
summary: Candidates commonly report that Zomato's engineering interviews combine coding and problem-solving rounds with a design round, often on delivery, search or restaurant-discovery problems, and that some roles also meet a hiring manager or the founder's office. Interviewers tend to look for ownership, speed and a clear product opinion. Zomato is part of Eternal, which also runs Blinkit, District and Hyperpure.
rounds: Hiring manager / founder's office round (some roles)
looks_for: A clear product opinion, backed by how you'd measure it
Thinking about restaurants and delivery partners, not only customers

questions.text: How would you design a system to show restaurants near a user, sorted by delivery time?
covers: Finding restaurants within reach: a geo index and each restaurant's delivery area
Estimating delivery time per restaurant from preparation time, partner availability and distance
Keeping it fast: caching by area, and updating when a restaurant closes or gets busy

questions.text: Tell me about something you built because you thought it should exist.
covers: The problem you noticed and who had it
How you built it, with little or no one asking you to
Who used it and what you learned from them

questions.text: What would you improve in the Zomato app, and how would you measure it?
covers: A specific flow and the user problem with it, from your own use
The change you'd make and what you'd leave out
One main metric and a guardrail, such as order conversion and cancellations

questions.text: Tell me about a time you worked a problem out from first principles instead of copying how others did it.
covers: The usual approach and why it didn't fit your case
How you broke the problem down to basics
What you built and how it compared with the usual way

questions.text: Describe a mistake of yours that reached users. How did you handle it?
covers: What went wrong, owned in the first person
How quickly you found it, fixed it and told people
What you changed so it wouldn't happen again

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to deliver with very little guidance. How did you decide what to do first?
covers: What was unclear and what was at stake
How you set priorities and who you checked with
The result, and what you'd do the same way again

questions.text: How would you design search in a food app so that a misspelt dish, a cuisine and a restaurant name all return useful results?
covers: Indexing dishes, restaurants and cuisines together
Typos, Hindi or regional spellings typed in English, and synonyms
Ranking by availability, distance and the user's past orders, within a tight time limit

questions.text: How would you design restaurant ratings and reviews so they are hard to fake?
covers: Linking reviews to real orders and weighting recent ones
Signals of abuse: new accounts, bursts of reviews, repeated text
Moderation and a way for restaurants to report unfair reviews

questions.text: Walk me through how a ten-minute grocery order could work, from tap to doorstep. Where would you focus engineering effort?
covers: Picking the store by stock and distance, then picking and packing inside it
Assigning a rider who is already near the store
Measuring each step to find the slowest one, and alerts when a store falls behind

questions.text: Restaurants in one city say new orders appear late on their devices. How would you debug it?
covers: Confirming scope: which restaurants, devices or app versions, since when
Tracing an order through each step, from order service to notification to the device
The fix, plus monitoring of order-to-restaurant delay

questions.text: Explain caching to a product manager. When could a cache show customers wrong information?
covers: A plain-words explanation with an everyday example
Stale data: a changed menu price or a closed restaurant still showing
Fixes: short expiry times or clearing the cache when the data changes

questions.text: How would you decide whether to lower the delivery fee in a city? What would you measure?
covers: The goal: more orders, new users or winning back lapsed ones
Who pays for the cut and what it does to margins
A test in some areas first, with guardrails such as partner earnings and delivery times

questions.text: Why Zomato, and why this team in particular?
covers: Something specific about the team's problem or product
What you bring that fits it, with an example
What you want to learn there

questions.text: Which Eternal business interests you most (Zomato, Blinkit, District or Hyperpure), and why?
covers: A clear pick and what you understand about its customers
A problem in it you'd like to work on
How your skills fit that problem

tips: Have a product opinion about their app.
Use the app as a customer the week before and note one thing that annoyed you and how you'd fix it.
In design rounds, treat restaurants and delivery partners as users of the system too, not only customers.
For founder's office or business roles, expect open problems; structure your answer and end with a recommendation, not a list.
Expect to be asked why something should be built at all; start from the user problem before the architecture.
